scenes.say: Your phone knows where you are to within a few metres. But it never sends a single signal to space. So how does it do that?
scenes.title: How does *GPS* find you?
scenes.subtitle: Satellites, clocks and a little geometry

scenes.say: Here is the surprising part. Your phone only listens. GPS satellites are constantly broadcasting, and your phone simply picks up what they shout.
There are about thirty one GPS satellites in orbit, around twenty thousand kilometres above the Earth.
scenes.label: GPS satellites, about 20,000 km up

scenes.say: GPS began as a military project in the nineteen seventies. In two thousand, the United States switched off a deliberate error that made civilian positions less accurate, and car navigation took off.
scenes.label: the year full accuracy opened to everyone

scenes.say: Each satellite repeats a simple message. It says who it is, exactly where it is, and the precise time it sent the message.
scenes.heading: Every message says

items.text: The precise time it was sent

scenes.say: That message takes about seven hundredths of a second to reach you. It is a tiny gap, but your phone can measure it very precisely.
scenes.label: for a signal to reach your phone

scenes.say: When the message arrives, your phone compares the send time with its own clock. The tiny delay tells it how far away that satellite is.
scenes.heading: Time becomes distance

scenes.say: When your phone first switches on, it does not know which satellites are overhead. It downloads a rough timetable called the almanac, guesses which satellites to listen for, and then locks on.
scenes.heading: Finding the satellites

scenes.say: Phones cheat a little. Instead of waiting minutes for the almanac from space, they fetch it over the internet in seconds. That is called assisted GPS, and it is why your map is ready almost instantly.
scenes.heading: Why your map is ready so fast

scenes.say: Radio travels at the speed of light, so a delay of one millionth of a second means about three hundred metres.
One distance puts you somewhere on a giant sphere. A second satellite narrows that to a circle. A third leaves just two points, and one of them is out in space.
scenes.heading: Narrowing it down

scenes.say: There is a catch. Satellites carry atomic clocks, but your phone has a cheap quartz clock that drifts. So your phone listens to a fourth satellite and solves for its own clock error too.
scenes.heading: The clock problem

scenes.say: Even Einstein shows up. Clocks in orbit tick slightly faster than clocks on the ground, so engineers correct for relativity every single day.
Without that correction, your position would drift by about ten kilometres a day.
scenes.label: of drift per day without relativity

scenes.say: By the time a signal reaches you, it is fainter than the background noise around it. Your phone digs it out by searching for a known pattern that each satellite repeats over and over.
GPS is American, but it is not alone. Europe runs Galileo, Russia runs GLONASS, and China runs BeiDou. Modern phones listen to all of them at once.
scenes.heading: Not just GPS

scenes.say: In big cities, signals bounce off tall buildings before they reach you, which adds extra delay. That is why your blue dot sometimes jumps across the street.
On a good day, with a clear view of the sky, your phone knows where you are to within about five metres.
scenes.label: typical phone accuracy under open sky

scenes.say: So, to recap. Satellites broadcast time and position. Your phone turns delays into distances. Four distances pin down where you are.
scenes.heading: Recap

scenes.say: And because your phone only listens, the satellites never learn where you are. Apps that share your location do that separately, over the internet.
And that's GPS. Next time your map snaps to your street, you'll know about the clocks in the sky. Thanks for watching.
scenes.title: GPS, explained
